prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

That is, groups of similar constructs were created and labelled and further specified, extended, split, or merged in the course of categorization until all constructs were assigned in satisfactory categories. For this categorization, only the constructs’ names were used, not the ratings. To validate the categories, the assignment of the constructs to the categories was repeated separately by rater A and a third rater C. These assignments were then compared to the first assignment to calculate the intrarater and the interrater reliability, respectively. Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.

Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).

First, the elicited constructs were categorized in terms of content by two raters (A and B), similar to the method of the Inductive Category Formation by Mayring (2014). That is, groups of similar constructs were created and labelled and further specified, extended, split, or merged in the course of categorization until all constructs were assigned in satisfactory categories. For this categorization, only the constructs’ names were used, not the ratings. To validate the categories, the assignment of the constructs to the categories was repeated separately by rater A and a third rater C. These assignments were then compared to the first assignment to calculate the intrarater and the interrater reliability, respectively. The intrarater reliability described by Cohen’s Kappa gave κ =0.895 which is an “almost perfect” (Landis & Koch, 1977, p.165) agreement. With regard to the interrater reliability, κ =0.802 indicates a “substantial” (Landis & Koch, 1977, p.165) agreement. The further analyses were based on the second assignment of rater A. One crossing in the hospital corridor only involved interactions with bicycles because the crosswalk traversed the bicycle lane but not the motor vehicle lanes. The cameras were oriented to capture the motor vehicle or bicycle approach to the crosswalk. Video quality was limited to maintain privacy of road users due to City policy. Data were collected for six hours (8–10 h, 11–13 h, and 16–18 h) on three weekdays in September through December 2018 at each location. The video recording times were selected based on peak expected combined volumes of pedestrians, bicycles, and motor vehicles, with a target of observing 200 pedestrian crossings with interactions from each location. Video data were manually reviewed to identify potential interactions of crossing pedestrians with motor vehicles or bicycles, defined using a conservative threshold of approximately 5 s passing time. Passing time (sometimes referred to as post encroachment time) is the time gap between when the first road user exits the point at which their paths intersect and when the second road user enters it. Although no conflict indicator completely captures risk, passing time is the most popular measure for studies of crossing pedestrians and other road users on transverse trajectories (Mahmud et al., 2017). A total of 4428 potential pedestrian interactions were identified: 3176 (72%) with motor vehicles and 1252 (28%) with bicycles. Due to the time cost of coding interactions, a random sample of 50 pedestrian crossings with interactions was selected from each location (except for the one low-volume location that had only 36), giving 536 crossings for further analysis. These 536 crossings were then stratified on combinations of passing time (<2, 2–3, 3–4 s) and interacting road user type (bicycles, motor vehicles, or both), which were both manually coded (see Table 1).
